paragraphs.source_en: The palynological study revealed a very narrow spectrum of plants in the inner part of the cave (Castelletti et al. 1998). This was attributed to a specific type of plant, gathered and brought by man into the part of the cave where the mouflon were presumably kept. Interestingly, the dung contains a high percentage of Echium pollen, which is a toxic plant. Although I do not exclude that there were also practical reasons for hunting, keeping and depicting mouflon, I argue that there are mainly ideological reasons at the very foundation of this phenomenon. Rituals involving wild animals, especially eland, and narcotic plants, are known from the ethnographic record (Lewis-Williams 1981).

paragraphs.source_en: Since no systematic excavation has been done on the Tassili Plateau we do not know if the same predominance of mouflon remains also occurs in the Tassilian rock art sites. This area contains the largest concentration of mouflon images and it is therefore important to compare the paintings with the archaeological record. It is quite surprising that in the Acacus mouflon are abundant in the archaeological record but rather rare in the paintings. According to Di Lernia (1999) mouflon do not seem to be relevant in the ideology of the groups in the Acacus, due to its scarcity in the rock art. I do not think this is the case. The Round Head art is rather homogeneous across the whole area which may suggest the same ideological foundation for all the groups.
